author: blu
body: Runs the IR-to-IR passes as an ordered pipeline. The pipeline is data -- a list of pass names -- so a pass can be switched off, reordered, or ablated by editing one list instead of rethreading a call chain. Dispatch is deliberately by name rather than through function-valued record fields: one list names the passes, one function maps a name to its transform, and nothing else has to exist for a pass to be registered.

author: blu
body: `ir-check` is a checker in a rewriter's clothing. It is registered like any other pass so it can be placed anywhere -- and more than once -- in the pipeline: `passes=fold-constants,ir-check,inline-leaf-calls, ir-check` brackets each rewriter with a validation of what it produced. It returns the chapter unchanged and reports through the violation channel instead. It is deliberately NOT in `default-ir-pipeline`: the shipping compiler pays nothing for a validator it never runs, and the validator is wanted exactly when a pass is under suspicion.

author: blu
body: `occ-report` is the same shape, but on the OTHER channel: an analysis wearing a rewriter's clothing. It runs the occurrence analyser (`occ-report-chapter`) over every definition and returns the chapter UNCHANGED, reporting each definition's per-binder classifications -- one `OCC <def>: name=Class, name=Class` line per definition -- as **infos, not violations**. That distinction is the whole reason the result carries two lists. `ir-check`'s findings are errors: malformed IR means the binary is not the program, so the compile halts. `occ-report`'s findings are information about well-formed IR, so they ride the info channel, do not halt, and never claim to be an error -- running `-Passes occ-report` reports the classifications AND still emits a binary. It exists so the analyser can be driven over real lowered IR and its answers read from the compile log, before any pass consumes them. Like `ir-check` it is NOT in `default-ir-pipeline`.

author: blu
body: `simplify` is a real rewriter -- the GHC-style simplifier (`IR/Simplify.codex`) -- that folds constants, propagates literals, and takes the known arm of a decided `if`, iterated to a fixpoint. It returns the rewritten chapter AND, on the info channel, one line with its rewrite count, so `-Passes simplify` both transforms the program and reports how much it did. It is opt-in and NOT in `default-ir-pipeline`: it absorbs the rules of the hardcoded `fold-constants` pass but does not yet replace it, so the shipping compiler's output is unchanged until that swap lands as its own CL.

author: blu
body: `inline-single-caller` is phase 2 of inlining (`IR/Lowering.codex`). It inlines a definition referenced exactly once in the chapter, which costs no duplication and lets emit-time dead-code elimination drop the original, so it admits a wider body shape than `inline-leaf-calls` does. It IS in `default-ir-pipeline`, and unlike `simplify` it did not wait behind a flag.

author: blu
body: The argument for leaving it off was that it does nothing for the compiler. That was a misreading of one metric: the deck does not move, but ten kilobytes come off the binary. A capability behind a flag is a capability the next person does not know to ask for, and finding it switched off years later with no reason recorded is worse than either shipping it or deleting it.

author: blu
body: `inline-cost-based` (`IR/Lowering.codex`) inlines a body of at most `inline-cost-ceiling` operation nodes at every saturated call site, whatever its reference count -- the first pass that duplicates on purpose. It is opt-in (`passes=+inline-cost-based`) and deliberately NOT in `default-ir-pipeline`, and unlike `simplify` the reason is a measurement, recorded at the ceiling constant in `Core/BuildSettings.codex`: on the selfhost every ceiling grew the binary and none made the compiled compiler faster. Building it also surfaced the template-reuse hazard `subst-once`'s record arm now guards against, which phase 2 could reach through nothing but a census miss; that account is at `subst-once`.

author: blu
body: Each violation is tagged with the slot that produced it, so a pipeline carrying `ir-check` twice says which of the two fired -- that is the whole point of the exercise, attributing malformed IR to the pass that made it. A pass that reports nothing costs nothing here: the tagging loop sees an empty list and returns.

author: blu
body: The per-pass frontier marks are behind `trace` and not on by default, because an info line reaches every compile log: `PIPELINE` already does, and three `.expected` files in the tree capture it. Three more lines per compile would have to be rewritten into all of them, which is a lot of churn to carry for an instrument that is read during an investigation and ignored the rest of the time.

author: blu
body: What the marks answer. In the FRONTEND, `-Measure` and `-IrCce` differ only by this pipeline: `emit-measure` calls `compile-frontend` and `emit-ir-cce` calls `compile-frontend-ir`, both are `compile-frontend-passes` with `run-passes` False and True, and `lower-chapter` sits ABOVE that branch, so lowering runs in both. They differ a second time after the frontend, in what they emit, and that half is not what these marks measure.

author: blu
body: The pipeline arrives on the mode line as `passes=name,name` -- comma separated, no spaces -- and the split lives here so the grammar sits beside the registry it names. The knob is the ablation surface: a pass that cannot be switched off cannot be measured, and the middle-end campaign scores pipeline configurations against each other rather than trusting any pass on reputation.
